frequency_question: How often does structural friction (fear of systemic financial destabilization, severe diplomatic retaliation, or fracture of correspondent banking networks) successfully deter the US Treasury from executing threatened major sanctions on systemically vital foreign entities?
membership_rule: Includes formal deliberations or explicit high-level Treasury threats regarding tier-1 foreign banks of major geopolitical rivals (China, Russia, EU-level states) where implementation was openly debated; excludes minor secondary sanctions on obscure shell companies or negligible firms.

cases.name: Standard Chartered / Iran sanctions waiver era threat
Russian Sberbank / VTB full blocking sanctions
Threatened sanctions on major Chinese banks over Hong Kong/Xinjiang

coverage_note: 4 instances enumerated capturing major systemic threat balance; small sample due to rarity of tier-1 targets.
known_gaps: Classified internal Treasury deliberations on avoided actions are uncounted.
skeleton: Total major tier-1 foreign financial institution threatened vs actually fully sanctioned with lethal correspondent banking bans over geopolitical friction points.
multiplier: 2 hits / 4 instances where structural friction of systemic disruption was acutely weighed
validity_reason: Structural friction models for superpower financial dominance remain stable until de-dollarization structurally erodes US leverage.
